svg.aria-label: A myeloma cell drawn with a phospholipid-bilayer membrane, showing how each treatment attacks it. Inside: bortezomib blocks the barrel-shaped proteasome, lenalidomide binds cereblon, next to the nucleus. Embedded in the membrane are CD38, BCMA and GPRC5D receptors. Daratumumab (an IgG antibody) binds CD38; a T cell's CAR binds BCMA; a bispecific antibody bridges the T cell to GPRC5D; dexamethasone is broadly toxic. Below, a separate subfigure shows melphalan, an older chemotherapy, crosslinking the two strands of the DNA double helix so the cell can no longer copy its DNA to divide — a blunt attack that harms every dividing cell, not just myeloma.
svg.text: How each treatment attacks the myeloma cell
bridges a T cell to GPRC5D
chemically damages DNA, so the cell can no longer divide
the trade-off: it harms every dividing cell, not just myeloma
